lede: Living things need nitrogen to build protein, but the nitrogen in the air is useless to them until bacteria change it. Four processes move nitrogen round the soil, each carried out by its own type of bacteria, and how wet the soil is decides which of them wins.
can: Name the four processes and the type of bacteria for each.
Explain why a waterlogged soil loses nitrate.
Say what a plant uses nitrate for and read a fertiliser chart.

md: Four-fifths of the air is nitrogen and plants cannot use any of it. Bacteria in the soil do the conversion for them, turning nitrogen gas into nitrate, while other bacteria turn it back again.

alt: The nitrogen cycle drawn as seven boxes joined by eight arrows. Nitrogen gas in the air becomes nitrates in the soil by nitrogen fixation carried out by nitrogen-fixing bacteria and by lightning. Nitrates are absorbed by roots and used to make protein in plants. Feeding passes that protein to animals. Death, excretion and egestion send protein to dead matter and waste. Decomposition by decomposing bacteria and fungi turns it into ammonium compounds. Nitrification by nitrifying bacteria turns ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates. Denitrification by denitrifying bacteria turns nitrates back into nitrogen gas in waterlogged, anaerobic conditions. A footnote marks nitrite and lightning as background beyond this specification.

title: The one rule that carries this topic
md:
**Learn every arrow as a pair: the process, and the bacteria.**

• **nitrogen fixation** — *nitrogen-fixing* bacteria
• **decomposition** — *decomposing* (saprophytic) bacteria and fungi
• **nitrification** — *nitrifying* bacteria
• **denitrification** — *denitrifying* bacteria

The names of individual species are **not** required. What is required is the ability to give the process in one part and the type of bacteria in the next, without swapping them over.

prompt: Bacteria that change nitrogen gas from the air into nitrates are called ______ bacteria.
explain: Nitrogen-fixing. Fixing means taking something out of the air and locking it into a compound — the same word is used for carbon fixation in photosynthesis.

text: The four processes, one at a time

md: **1 Nitrogen fixation.** The air is about four-fifths **nitrogen gas**, but plants cannot use it: the molecule is too unreactive. **nitrogen-fixing bacteria** turn it into **nitrates**, which plants can absorb. Some live free in the soil; others live inside **root nodules** on the roots of **legumes** — clover, peas, beans — where they get sugars from the plant and give it nitrate in return. **Lightning** fixes a little nitrogen too.

alt: Close-up photograph of a legume root system lifted from the soil. Pale branching roots carry a scattering of rounded, pinkish-brown swellings a few millimetres across, spaced along the thicker roots, with fine root hairs and soil grains around them
caption: Root nodules on a legume, lifted straight out of the soil. Each pinkish swelling is a chamber full of nitrogen-fixing bacteria that the plant houses and feeds.
prompt: Name the type of bacteria living inside these swellings, name the process they carry out, and state what the plant gains from housing them.

title: Why a plant cannot use the nitrogen it is standing in
md: Nitrogen gas is two atoms locked together so tightly that nothing in a plant can pull them apart. Plants need nitrogen as **nitrate** instead, a soluble ion the roots can absorb and build into amino acids.

prompt: Where on a clover plant do the nitrogen-fixing bacteria live?
explain: In root nodules on the roots of legumes — clover, peas and beans.

md: **2 Decomposition.** When plants and animals die, and whenever animals produce **urine and faeces**, the **protein** and **urea** in that material is broken down by **decomposing (saprophytic) bacteria and fungi** into **ammonium compounds** in the soil. This is the step that Summer 2025's candidates most often left unnamed.

prompt: Which process turns the protein in dead material into ammonium compounds?
explain: Decomposition, by saprophytic bacteria and fungi.

md: **3 Nitrification.** **nitrifying bacteria** oxidise those **ammonium compounds** into **nitrites** and then into **nitrates**. They are **aerobic**, so they need soil with **air spaces** — which is why a waterlogged field makes less nitrate as well as losing what it has.

**4 Denitrification.** **denitrifying bacteria** do the opposite: they turn **nitrates back into nitrogen gas**, which is lost to the air. They are **anaerobic**, so they multiply exactly where the others are struggling — in **waterlogged soil**.

alt: A five-column table with one row for each of nitrogen fixation, decomposition, nitrification and denitrification, giving what each changes, what it changes into, the type of bacteria and whether air is needed. Only denitrification is marked as not needing air. A footnote marks nitrite as background beyond this specification.

prompt: Which process turns ammonium compounds into nitrates?
explain: Nitrification, by nitrifying bacteria. Denitrification runs the other way and produces nitrogen gas; decomposition is the step before, which makes the ammonium in the first place.

title: GCSE Biology Revision The Nitrogen Cycle (Triple)
why: The whole cycle built up arrow by arrow in a few minutes, with the bacteria named at each step. Watch it, then answer the question underneath from memory.

prompt: Bacteria that turn nitrates back into nitrogen gas are called ______ bacteria.
explain: Denitrifying — de- meaning taking away. They are anaerobic, so waterlogged soil is where they do most damage to a farmer's nitrate.

md:
Write the waterlogging answer as a **chain**, one link per mark:

**1** The soil is waterlogged, so the **air spaces are full of water**.
**2** There is therefore **little or no oxygen** — conditions are **anaerobic**.
**3** **Nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria are aerobic**, so they become less active and **less nitrate is made**.
**4** **Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic**, so they multiply and **turn more nitrate into nitrogen gas**.
**5** So there is **less nitrate available to plants**, and less protein can be made.

prompt: Why is a waterlogged soil short of oxygen?
options: the plants use it all up
it is too cold for air to dissolve
explain: Water fills the spaces between the soil grains, so conditions become anaerobic.

title: March 2026 B1 Higher Q7 — the hardest question on the paper
md: Parts (d) and (e) asked candidates to **name the types of nitrogen bacteria** and **explain why waterlogged soil leaves plants short of nitrate**. The Chief Examiner reported both as the most challenging on the paper, and added that in part (d) **candidates lost marks by naming the processes when the question asked for the types of bacteria**. Read the command word twice: *nitrification* and *nitrifying bacteria* are not interchangeable.

prompt: Why does a waterlogged field lose nitrate?
options: the air spaces fill with water, so anaerobic denitrifying bacteria thrive and turn nitrate into nitrogen gas
the nitrate is washed downwards out of reach of the roots only
the nitrifying bacteria turn the nitrate back into ammonium
answer: the air spaces fill with water, so anaerobic denitrifying bacteria thrive and turn nitrate into nitrogen gas
explain: Leaching does happen, but the answer the scheme wants is the bacteria: no oxygen means denitrifying bacteria multiply, and nitrate leaves as nitrogen gas. Nitrifying bacteria never run backwards.

md: Plants absorb **nitrates** through their roots and use them to make **amino acids** and then **proteins** — for growth, for enzymes, for everything. More nitrate therefore means more growth, until the plants cannot take in any more. Here the yield climbs by **50%** from no fertiliser to low, and by **25%** from low to medium, but only by **0.2 tonnes per hectare** from medium to high. The reason for the flat top is exactly the sentence March 2026's report says only the more able candidates wrote: **the plants cannot absorb any more nitrate**.

prompt: The yield rose from 4.8 to 6 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase.
explain: (6 − 4.8) ÷ 4.8 × 100 = 1.2 ÷ 4.8 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by 6 instead would give 20%, which is the error the March 2026 report names.

title: Not on this specification
md: You do **not** need the names of individual bacteria (*Rhizobium*, *Nitrosomonas*, *Nitrobacter*), the chemical equations of any of these reactions, the Haber process, or eutrophication as part of *this* outcome — eutrophication is outcome 1.7.12 and has its own topic. What you do need is the four processes, the four types of bacteria, and the aerobic or anaerobic condition each one needs.

Name the four processes and the **type of bacteria** for each.
Say what **nitrogen fixation** makes and where **root nodules** are.
Explain why a **waterlogged** soil loses nitrate.
Say what a plant uses **nitrates** for.
Calculate a percentage increase from a yield chart.

Higher only, and it has carried a whole question in each of the last three series. The schemes are strict about the **-ing** and **-ation** endings, and the waterlogging explanation is marked as a chain, one mark per link. Stuck: name the process and the microorganism that carries it out, then say what it turns into what.
